paper_metadata.title: QEA-FAD: Quantum Enhanced Autoencoders For Anomaly Detection in Finance and Healthcare

summary: The paper presents QEA-FAD, a gate-based quantum autoencoder framework for anomaly detection on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset and credit card fraud data. Reported quantitative results include 0.845 split threshold and 0.9 malign-classification accuracy for the proposed breast-cancer ansatz, 0.99 split / 0.24 accuracy for the Bravo-Prieto baseline, 0.96 split / 0.81 accuracy for the Romero baseline, and fraud-detection compression fidelities of 0.89 for non-fraudulent versus 0.66 for fraudulent transactions, with additional results on IBM Guadalupe and Rigetti Aspen-11 hardware.

experiments.description: Quantum autoencoder anomaly detection on the Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) dataset using the proposed QEA-FAD ansatz, evaluated in Qiskit simulation and on IBM QPU hardware.

algorithm.variant: Quantum autoencoder (QAE) with entanglement-assisted encoder-decoder; proposed QEA-FAD first ansatz
algorithm.ansatz: Amplitude embedding encoder + angle embedding encoder; dual-encoder design with two CNOT interactions between latent space and trash qubit
algorithm.convergence_criteria: trained until maximum fidelity for normal data / trash qubits reset to |0...0>

hyperparameters.dataset_features_used: 32 features or top 8 most relevant features

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Breast cancer feature vectors are encoded into quantum states; paper states amplitude embedding for the first encoder and angle embedding for the second encoder
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize reconstruction error / maximize compression fidelity for normal data; anomalies identified by low fidelity of trash qubits relative to |00...00>
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Trash qubits are reset to |0...0>; anomaly decision by fidelity thresholding

problem_instance.description: Breast cancer anomaly detection (malignant vs benign cell classification)

dataset_specification.description: 569 samples; 30 original numerical features plus 2 engineered features ('under average' and 'over average'); experiments used all 32 features or top 8 most relevant ones

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Engineered two additional features representing deviations beyond two standard deviations; feature selection to top 8 in some experiments
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Histogram-based compression fidelity analysis; split threshold 0.845; accuracy reported for malign classification; comparison across simulation and IBM QPU hardware

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Feature engineering and feature selection on breast cancer dataset
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compression fidelity histograms; threshold-based classification using split value 0.845

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: Compression fidelity and loss curves shown over epochs

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: No asymptotic speedup or crossover analysis; only small-scale QAE anomaly detection on breast cancer data with simulation and IBM QPU comparison
limiting_factors: No demonstrated quantum advantage over classical autoencoders
No complexity analysis or crossover size reported
Hardware results are small-scale NISQ demonstrations
Performance is threshold-based classification rather than end-to-end advantage

notes: Paper explicitly reports Qiskit simulation and IBM QPU hardware results, but does not name the exact IBM device in the breast-cancer experiment section.
Number of qubits, circuit depth, and parameter count are not explicitly stated in the provided text; nulls retained.
No asymptotic complexity or speedup order is characterized in the paper; speedup_order set to none_proven by inference from absence of analysis.
Authors report 0.9 accuracy on malign classification and compare against classical autoencoders, but do not establish quantum advantage.
IBM QPU and Qiskit simulation are used for feasibility, not advantage demonstration.
